text.title: Niche Scorecard Core Rules
text.summary: 7 testable rules for constructing a weighted niche scorecard that actually discriminates: frozen weights with real spread, independent criteria, hard gates evaluated outside the weighted sum, every score anchored to a measured quantity, and a sensitivity check the winner must survive.

rule.statement: `criteria` weights MUST sum to 1.0, be written before the first niche is scored, and be identical for every niche in the comparison. A per-niche weight vector, or any weight edited after scores became visible, invalidates the artefact.

rationale.source: Pre-registration of decision criteria — MCDA practice

rule.rationale: Weights tuned once the scores are on screen turn the scorecard into a defence of a choice already made. And if each niche carries its own weights, the totals are measured on different yardsticks — which destroys the only property the totals were computed for, comparability.

rule.statement: The largest weight MUST be at least twice the smallest. A near-uniform vector (for example 0.22 / 0.20 / 0.20 / 0.20 / 0.18) is rejected and the analyst must re-derive weights that express a real priority ordering.
rule.rationale: With near-uniform weights the weighted total collapses to the arithmetic mean of five noisy 1-10 judgements. The gap between the top two niches then falls inside single-criterion scoring error, so the ranking reports the analyst's rounding, not a property of the niches.

rule.statement: No two criteria may be scored from the same underlying quantity. If Market Size and Profitability are both derived from one revenue estimate, one of them must be re-anchored (for example Profitability to gross margin or median deal size) or dropped.
rule.rationale: Two criteria fed by one number act as a single criterion carrying the sum of both weights. The intended 25/20 split silently becomes a 45 on one signal, and a niche that is large but structurally unprofitable wins on the strength of one input counted twice.

rule.statement: Knock-out conditions — a licensing or regulatory barrier the founder cannot clear, no reachable acquisition channel, a legal bar to operating in the market — MUST be evaluated first and set `decision` to `reject` outright. They never enter `scores` and never receive a weight.

rationale.source: MCDA — conjunctive (non-compensatory) screening before compensatory aggregation

rule.rationale: A weighted sum is compensatory by construction: a 9 on Market Size arithmetically cancels a 1 on Barriers. The scorecard then recommends, with a high total, a niche the founder is not permitted to enter — the one failure mode a total score can never surface.

rule.statement: Every 1-10 score MUST cite the observable it was derived from plus its source: SAM in currency for Market Size, count of funded direct competitors for Competition, median deal size or gross margin for Profitability, months to first revenue for Barriers.
rule.rationale: An unanchored 1-10 is a confidence rating dressed as a measurement. The same analyst scores the same niche differently on two different days, so re-running the scorecard after new evidence cannot distinguish a real change in the niche from drift in the analyst.

rule.statement: The "Your Fit" criterion MUST be scored from artefacts — things shipped in the domain, years worked in it, existing audience or client list — never from self-reported interest or enthusiasm.
rule.rationale: This is the one criterion whose scorer is also its subject, so self-rated fit clusters at 8-10 across every candidate niche. A criterion that is near-constant contributes nothing to the ranking, which means its 15% weight is discarded and the decision is actually made by the remaining 85%.

rule.statement: Before writing `decision`, perturb each weight by ±20% relative, renormalize to 1.0, and re-rank. If the top niche changes under any single perturbation, report a tie and route to a tiebreak on fresh evidence rather than declaring a winner.

rationale.source: Sensitivity analysis in multi-criteria decision analysis

rule.rationale: Weights are judgement, not measurement, and are rarely defensible to better than a fifth of their value. A ranking that flips inside that band is reporting the analyst's weight guess; committing a quarter of roadmap to it is committing to a coin flip that looks like arithmetic.
